Subject:       Emergency License Amendment Request: One-Time-Use Amendment to Allow
               Alternative Fuel Handling Method for the Recovery of Fuel Assembly DD41


Pursuant to Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) 50.90 and 10 CFR 50.91(a)(5)
Palisades Energy, LLC (Palisades Energy) hereby requests a one-time emergency change to
the Renewed Facility Operating License (RFOL) for Palisades Nuclear Plant (PNP). The license
amendment request (LAR) proposes to revise UFSAR Sections 9.11 Fuel Handling and Storage
Systems, and 14.19 Fuel Handling Accident, to facilitate transport of a fuel assembly from the
reactor utilizing different plant equipment and following a different travel path than is described
within the UFSAR.
Palisades entered Mode 6 (Refueling) and began loading fuel into the reactor vessel on August
30, 2026. During core reload, fuel assembly DD41 (DD41) was placed into core location H-1
and tilted over after being released by the refueling machine. DD41 is currently oriented at an
approximate 30-degree angle with the lower tie plate in core location H-1 and the upper tie plate
leaning against the core shroud on the opposite side of the core.
The proposed UFSAR changes would be effective for the duration of the recovery of the DD41
fuel assembly including its safe retrieval from its current orientation in the reactor vessel,
packaging it within an engineered transfer canister, transporting the canister from the
containment building to the spent fuel handling building, and placement of the canister and fuel
assembly into the cask loading area within the spent fuel pool.
Emergency approval of the proposed licensing basis change is justified to restore the DD41 fuel
assembly to an appropriate location in the spent fuel pool in an expedited manner. Therefore,
Palisades Energy requests an approval date of October 2, 2026, for this LAR.
The proposed changes have been evaluated in accordance with 10 CFR 50.91(a), Notice for
public comment, subparagraph (5), using the standards in 10 CFR 50.92, Issuance of
amendment, paragraph (c), and it has been determined that the changes involve no significant
hazards consideration. The basis for this determination is included in the Enclosure.

BACKGROUND
During core reload, fuel assembly DD41 (DD41) was placed into core location H-1 and tilted
over after being released by the refueling machine. DD41 is currently oriented at an
approximate 30-degree angle from the core plate, with the lower tie plate (LTP) in core location
H-1 and the upper tie plate (UTP) leaning against the core shroud on the opposite side of the
core. The fuel rods in DD41 retained their integrity as primary fission product barrier. None of
the other fuel assemblies in the reactor core were impacted by DD41.
DD41 is currently stable and no further movement has been detected. Compensatory measures
have been taken to stabilize the assembly to keep it from further movement, and the refueling
team has DD41 under continuous camera surveillance. The recovery evaluation determined that
damage to the DD41 UTP prevents use of the refueling machine to grapple DD41 in the manner
described in Updated Final Safety Analysis Report (UFSAR) Section 9.11, Fuel Handling and
Storage Systems (Section 9.11).
1      SUMMARY DESCRIPTION
In accordance with Title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR), 50.90, Application for
amendment of license, construction permit, or early site permit, Palisades Energy, LLC
(Palisades Energy), hereby requests U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) review and
approval of a license amendment request (LAR) for a one-time use emergency revision to the
Palisades Nuclear Plant (PNP) licensing basis to facilitate removal of the DD41 fuel assembly
from the reactor vessel. This LAR proposes no Technical Specification (TS) changes; however,
Attachment 1 contains proposed revisions to UFSAR Section 9.11, and UFSAR Section 14.19,
Fuel Handling Accident (Section 14.19), to define an alternative fuel handling method.
This change would only be effective for the duration of the recovery of DD41 including its safe
retrieval from its current orientation, packaging it within an engineered Fuel Transfer Canister
(FTC), transporting the canister from containment, and placement of the canister into the cask
loading area within the spent fuel pool.
Emergency approval of the proposed licensing basis change is justified to restore DD41 to an
appropriate location in the spent fuel pool in an expedited manner. Therefore, Palisades Energy
requests an approval date of October 2, 2026, for this license amendment request.
To facilitate recovery of DD41, Holtec Manufacturing engineered and fabricated a custom
recovery tool capable of engaging the fuel assembly and an engineered FTC to support and
enclose DD41 during transit from the reactor vessel to the spent fuel pool.
A detailed description and technical evaluation of the licensing basis requirements and the
proposed changes are provided in Sections 2 and 3 of this LAR.
The LAR addresses the applicable evaluation in Section 4, including applicable regulatory
requirements, and the No Significant Hazards consideration.
Environmental considerations are discussed in Section 5. It was determined that no
environmental impact statement or environmental assessment need be prepared in connection
with the proposed amendment.
 PNP 2026-052
Enclosure
Page 3 of 19

2       DETAILED DESCRIPTION
Palisades Energy proposes, on a one-time basis to revise the UFSAR Sections 9.11 and 14.19
to describe the DD41 recovery process due to the deviation from the approved licensing basis
that covers routine fuel movements. The approach and considerations for this process are
described in further detail in Section 2.3 of the LAR.
The UFSAR proposed changes are described in this Enclosure. The Technical Specifications
(TS) and TS Bases are not affected and do not require revision to support DD41 recovery
actions.
2.1     Current Licensing Basis Requirements
2.1.1   UFSAR Section 9.11, Fuel Handling and Storage Systems
UFSAR Section 9.11 of the PNP UFSAR describes the operation and requirements of the
handling and storage system for new and spent fuel. This section contains descriptions of the
structural analysis of the Spent Fuel Pool (SFP) and criticality prevention analysis, as well as
descriptions of the new fuel storage areas which will remain unchanged by this proposed
amendment.
UFSAR Section 9.11.3.5, Radiological Considerations, discusses radiological conditions during
refueling or fuel inspection activities and of the SFP. Personnel performing refueling or fuel
inspection activities are protected from excessive radiation levels by water shielding. Fuel
assemblies are maintained under at least 10 feet of water and individual fuel rods are
maintained under at least 8 feet of water. Equipment is designed and operated such that it is not
possible to lift irradiated fuel above the 10 feet submergence limit. Protection against accidental
radiation release from irradiated fuel is provided by the containment ventilation system and
isolation capability, if required, of the SFP and auxiliary building ventilation system. The
submergence of an assembly in 10 feet of water results in the dilution and partial retention of
released fission products by the pool water.
UFSAR Section 9.11.4, Fuel Handling System, describes the typical refueling process where
the fuel handling system transfers the fuel assemblies between the refueling cavity and the fuel
storage pool on fixed rails through a transfer tube. The refueling machine removes a spent fuel
assembly from the core, transports it to the tilt machine and deposits it in the transfer carriage
within the tilt machine. The carriage is then rotated from a vertical position to a horizontal
position and moved through the transfer tube to the spent fuel storage area. The carriage is
then rotated to a vertical position, the spent fuel removed and placed in a storage rack by the
service platform.
2.1.2   UFSAR Section 14.19 Fuel Handling Accident
UFSAR Section 14.19 describes the remote possibility of an accident with significant
consequences during refueling. Physical limitations imposed upon refueling operations and
administrative restrictions on refueling procedures reduce the possibility of an accident.
Fuel handling hoists and manipulators are designed so that it is not possible to raise fuel
bundles above a position which provides the minimum water shield requirements. This
constraint applies in fuel handling areas inside containment and in the SFP area. In addition to
these safeguards, direct radiation monitors at fuel handling areas give operating personnel
 PNP 2026-052
Enclosure
Page 4 of 19

audible and visual warning of high radiation levels. Interlocks are also provided to prevent tilt
machine rotation during insertion and removal of spent fuel assemblies. Fuel storage pool
integrity is assured by designing the pool and storage racks as Class 1 structures.
Per Section 14.19.3, Radiological Consequences, PNP is currently licensed for a fuel handling
accident of a dropped assembly during handling. The analysis postulates the assembly is
damaged to the extent that a number of fuel rods fail. A part of the licensing basis is an
independent calculation and assessment performed by the NRC which assumed all fuel rods
equivalent of an entire assembly failure of 216 rods occurred in comparison of the Consumer
Power Company’s analysis assumption that only 13 rods would fail in an outer row. The results
of the analysis of a dropped fuel assembly in the reactor core provides data that the energy
absorption capability of the fuel assemblies indicate that an assembly dropped in such manner
is capable of absorbing the kinetic energy of the drop without causing any fuel rod failures.
2.1.3   Technical Specifications
The PNP TS and associated Bases were reviewed to determine whether the proposed
alternative fuel handling process requires changes. The review considered TS applicability
during MODE 6, CORE ALTERATIONS, movement of irradiated fuel assemblies, movement of
a fuel cask in or over the SFP, and storage of irradiated fuel in the SFP.
The review determined that no changes to the TS requirements are necessary. All applicable
Limiting Conditions for Operation, Required Actions, Surveillance Requirements, Design
Features, and Administrative Controls will be satisfied during the proposed alternative fuel
handling evolution.
The proposed activity does, however, change certain assumptions and descriptions associated
with the existing fuel handling safety analysis in UFSAR Sections 9.11 and 14.19. In particular,
the current licensing basis describes irradiated fuel as remaining underwater during transfer and
credits the surrounding water for shielding, cooling, and retention of released iodine. The
proposed alternative fuel handling process uses an engineered FTC with associated approved
procedure controls during portions of the proposed activity in which the damaged fuel assembly
is not submerged. The corresponding FTC safety risk analysis demonstrates that applicable
radiological, criticality, thermal, structural, and fuel handling safety criteria continue to be
satisfied for the alternative method.
TS reviewed for applicability and determined to be impacted by the proposed changes to
UFSAR Sections 9.11 and 14.19 included the following TS:
   •    3.3.6, “Refueling Containment High Radiation (CHR) Instrumentation”
   •    3.7.10, “Control Room Ventilation (CRV) Filtration”
   •    3.7.11, “Control Room Ventilation (CRV) Cooling”
   •    3.7.12, “Fuel Handling Area Ventilation System”
   •    3.7.14, “Spent Fuel Pool (SFP) Water Level”
   •    3.7.15, “Spent Fuel Pool (SFP) Boron Concentration”
   •    3.7.16, “Spent Fuel Pool Storage”

Enclosure
Page 5 of 19

      •   3.9.3, “Containment Penetrations”
      •   3.9.6, “Refueling Cavity Water Level”
      •   4.3, “Fuel Storage”
The revised safety analysis does not alter the required operability, applicability, or actions
associated with these TS. Conforming changes to affected TS Bases are not appropriate due to
this being one-time operation limited to recovery of DD41.
UFSAR Section 9.11.3.2 currently identifies the Region 2 cask laydown area as an area that
may be used for placement of spent fuel shipping casks, dry fuel storage equipment, and fuel
inspection and repair equipment. The FTC containing DD41 will be temporarily staged in this
area as part of the approved recovery evolution. The revised UFSAR will specifically describe
this temporary configuration and the associated criticality, thermal, structural, radiological, and
load handling analyses.
Following transfer to the SFP, DD41 will be removed from the FTC and placed into an approved
storage configuration meeting the applicable requirements of TS 3.7.16 and TS 4.3 before
subsequent dry fuel storage activities.
2.2       Reason for the Proposed Change
Due to the conditions described in the Background section, DD41 cannot be recovered using
the refueling machine, and relocating DD41 from the reactor vessel to the spent fuel pool will
require a process not described in the UFSAR. PNP proposes a revision to UFSAR Sections
9.11 and 14.19 to implement a one-time alternative process that would relocate DD41 from the
reactor vessel to the SFP, where subsequent handling and storage can be performed using the
fuel-handling process described in the UFSAR.

The proposed activity changes the UFSAR-described fuel-handling process and associated
fuel-handling accident assumptions. UFSAR Section 9.11.3.5.1 describes personnel performing
refueling or fuel inspection activities as protected from excessive radiation levels by maintaining
fuel assemblies under at least 10 feet of water. UFSAR Section 9.11.4.1 describes fuel
assemblies as being handled underwater at all times using the refueling machine, tilt machines,
transfer carriage and rails, and spent fuel handling machine. UFSAR Section 14.19 assumes
adequate fuel cooling is provided by the surrounding water and states that fuel is not removed
from the water during transfer from the reactor core to its storage location. Section 14.19 further
assumes that fuel-gap activity from damaged fuel is released to refueling water and credits
partial iodine retention in that water. UFSAR Table 14.19-1 assumes a minimum of 22.5 feet of
water above the damaged fuel assembly. Section 14.19.1 further states that fuel-handling hoists
and manipulators are designed such that fuel assemblies cannot be raised above the position
necessary to maintain the minimum water-shield requirement.

The alternative recovery process departs from these assumptions by transferring DD41 above
water within a drained FTC using the containment polar crane, purpose-designed rigging, a rail
transfer system through the equipment hatch, and the SFP building crane. The revised safety
analysis therefore establishes the safety basis for the alternative recovery process by evaluating
 PNP 2026-052
Enclosure
Page 6 of 19

radiological consequences, decay-heat removal and fuel temperatures, criticality, structural
integrity, shielding, and postulated load drops and lifting-system failures.

PNP applied the 10 CFR 50.59 process to evaluate the proposed process for DD41 recovery
and determined that prior NRC approval is required to proceed with the proposed use of the
FTC alternative fuel-handling process.

2.3     Description of the Proposed Change
PNP proposes revisions to UFSAR Sections 9.11 and 14.19 to describe an alternative fuel-
handling process. The process would be a one-time operation limited to recovery of DD41.
Once recovery of DD41 is completed, the changes would transition to historical UFSAR content.

The alternative fuel-handling process would lift DD41 using the Containment Polar Crane (L-1)
and purpose-designed fuel movement device (FMD) supported by slings and chain-falls to
remove the assembly from the reactor. Once removed from the reactor, DD41 would be loaded
underwater into the FTC staged on the reactor cavity floor. The FTC containing DD41 would be
lifted from the water, drained, and then transported through containment using the crane and
existing rail system along a lift path that exits through the containment equipment hatch into the
SFP area of the auxiliary building. Once in the SFP area, the FTC would be lifted using the Fuel
Pool Building Crane (L-3) and placed vertically in the Region 2 cask laydown area of the SFP.

All existing radiation protection analyses, heavy-load lift analyses, and procedures have been
reviewed and revised, as necessary, to incorporate requirements associated with this lift. These
changes would be incorporated into the applicable procedures before any fuel-handling activity
using the alternative process.

2.3.1   Summary of UFSAR Revised Text
All revisions to the UFSAR include a note that designates the language as historical UFSAR
content following the recovery of fuel assembly DD41.

Section 9.11.4 would be revised to include the following paragraphs:

        The Fuel Handling System has an additional transfer method for transferring damaged
        fuel assemblies that cannot be transferred using the normal process through the transfer
        tube. The additional transfer method is composed of an engineered Fuel Movement
        Device (FMD) used to engage and remove a damaged fuel assembly from the reactor
        core by lifting it and placing it into an engineered Fuel Transfer Canister (FTC) staged at
        the bottom of the refueling cavity away from the reactor flange. The FMD is attached to
        the polar crane with rigging components along with dynamometers to measure the
        physical force of the suspended load that provides live accurate measurements during
        the lift to operators. Once the FTC is assembled and ready to be lifted out of the water,
        the FTC with the assembly inside is lifted to the containment trolley system at the
        equipment hatch. Once loaded on the trolley, the FTC is moved out of the containment
        building through the equipment hatch into the spent fuel pool building.

Enclosure

       8.      Fuel Movement Device

       The Fuel Movement Device (FMD) is designed and fabricated to be submerged and
       operated remotely to safely grasp and lift the tilted fuel assembly from the reactor
       core. The FMD is rigged to the containment polar crane, L-1, for retrieval and
       subsequent movement to the engineered transfer canister. The FMD is classified as a
       non-safety related component to be used only for tilted fuel assembly DD41 recovery.
       The lifting operation utilizing the FMD, with the fuel assembly attached, occurs entirely
       underwater always maintaining at least 10 feet of water above the assembly. The
       allowable stress limits used in the design and analysis are per ASME Section III,
       Subsection NF for Class 3 linear supports. The calculated stresses in the FMD under
       normal lifting and handling conditions are compared against applicable Level A allowable
       stress limits. [Reference 1]

       The FMD has a total of 12 lift arms. Calculations conservatively assume that only 8 of 12
       lift arms are in contact with the fuel assembly during the lift (i.e., minimum of 4 lift arms
       at top and bottom ends with 2 lift arms in contact on each side of the fuel assembly).

       For purposes of defining the upper limit of the radiological consequences of a fuel-
       handling accident, Section 14.19 assumed that all fuel rods in the affected fuel assembly
       fail. Accordingly, the radiological consequences of fuel rod damage resulting from FMD
       fuel-handling accidents are bounded by the existing Section 14.19 fuel-handling accident
       analysis.

       9.      Fuel Transfer Canister

       The Fuel Transfer Canister (FTC) is an engineered Holtec designed enclosure fabricated
       to accommodate fuel assembly DD41. The enclosure fully protects the damaged
       assembly during transport. The enclosure has been analyzed for dropped load impact
       and radiation risks. [Reference 2]

       A shielding analysis calculation concludes that the enclosure will maintain dose rates
       below target rates of 500 mrem/hr on contact for the most limiting surface of the FTC.

Section 14.19.1 would be revised to include the following paragraphs:

       Due to the need to recover fuel assembly DD41 which tilted over after it was released by
       the fuel-handling machine grapple during refueling activities, additional consideration
       associated with activities related to tilted fuel assemblies is necessary to restore
       Palisades Unit 1 back to normal plant operations.
       Visual inspections of the tilted assembly concluded that damage sustained by the fuel
       assembly prevents retrieval using the grapple on the refueling machine. The specific
       conditions of the DD41 fuel assembly are that only assembly frame damage was
       sustained and that the primary fission product barrier of fuel cladding is still intact. The
       described condition remains bounded by the existing fuel handling accident described in
       Section 14.19.3. A retrieval process was developed to use specially designed and
       engineered recovery components described in Section 9.11 to retrieve the tilted fuel
       assembly.

        The retrieval process includes steps where the fuel assembly is transported out of the
        shielding water barrier protection. Transporting the assembly in an engineered fuel
        transfer canister has been analyzed against existing design and regulatory requirements
        by an engineering design package that addresses the risks and safety concerns. The
        various analyses performed to support the transport conclude that transporting through
        the containment hatch and into the fuel handling building is safe and does not violate
        any existing dose, seismic, Technical Specifications, UFSAR, Technical Specifications
        Bases, or any other design basis documents that currently make up the regulatory
        structure of the Palisades plant that are part of or referenced in the Renewed Facility
        Operating License (RFOL) or any of its conditions.
        Therefore, the recovery scheme to mitigate consequences and recover a damaged fuel
        assembly, that cannot be handled with the refueling machine grapple, has been
        determined to be within the regulatory framework of the current RFOL.
2.4     Basis for Emergency Processing
In 10 CFR 50.91(a)(5), the NRC refers to “emergency situations” as those in which failure to act
in a timely way would result in derating or shutdown of a nuclear power plant, or in prevention of
either resumption of operation or of increase in power output up to the plant’s licensed power
level. Under such a situation, the Commission may issue a license amendment involving no
significant hazards consideration without prior notice and opportunity for a hearing or public
comment.
Tilting of fuel assembly DD41 was not an intended outcome of core loading and therefore PNP
could not have foreseen the need for a license amendment to revise the UFSAR-described fuel-
handling process and associated fuel-handling accident assumptions that would support a
routine licensing amendment request submission schedule.
PNP is requesting emergency processing of this license amendment request as a delay in
approval of the proposed changes would result in a delay in the resumption of activities
necessary to reach the plant conditions required to restore the plant to power operation.
10 CFR 50.91(a)(7) states “Where the Commission finds that significant hazards considerations
are involved, it will issue a Federal Register notice providing an opportunity for a prior hearing
even in an emergency situation, unless it finds an imminent danger to the health or safety of the
public.” PNP concludes that the proposed amendment does not involve a significant hazards
consideration under the standards set forth in 10 CFR 50.92(c), and accordingly, a finding of no
significant hazards consideration is justified, as discussed in Section 4.2.
3       TECHNICAL EVALUATION
3.1     Recovery Equipment Description
3.1.1   Fuel Movement Device
PNP intends to attach an FMD to DD41 for stabilization and provide an alternative rigging
attachment point. The FMD enables use of L-1 in combination with two independent chain falls
to lift the FMD holding DD41 for removal from the reactor cavity and placement into the FTC.
 PNP 2026-052
Enclosure
Page 9 of 19

The FMD clasps around and reinforces DD41 at the grid straps, in contact with the guide bars,
forming a structural spine along the assembly. End clasps secure the top and bottom of DD41 to
prevent it from slipping from the FMD during lifting and handling.
The FMD lifts a single fuel assembly and is considered a “heavy load” per the definition in
Section 1.2 of NUREG-0612, Control of Heavy Loads at Nuclear Power Plants because the
combined weight of the FMD and DD41 is greater than the combined weight of a fuel assembly
and its associated handling tool at PNP (1300 lbs., Operating Requirements Manual Section
3.21). The lifting operation using the FMD would be performed underwater, with DD41
maintained at least 10 feet below the water surface, consistent with the radiation shielding
provisions described in UFSAR Section 9.11.3, Spent Fuel Storage.
The purpose of this calculation is to evaluate the structural integrity of the Fuel Movement
Device (FMD). The primary input data for stress analysis are dimensional data, weight data, and
construction materials, as well as fuel assembly geometry and weights. All calculated safety
factors are greater than 1.0, indicating that the stress criteria for ASME III Subsection NF for
Class 3 linear supports are satisfied.
3.1.2   Fuel Transfer Canister
Structural Evaluation
The applicable design and Level A service limits of ASME Section III, Subsection NF are
adopted as the basis for evaluating the FTC under normal lifting and handling conditions.
Calculated stresses include the specified dynamic load factor and are compared with the
allowable stresses applicable to the material, temperature, component, and stress category.
The ultimate-strength design factor of 10 specified in NUREG-0612, Section 5.1.6(3)(b), for
interfacing lift points was adopted for the combined static and dynamic lifting load.
Associated analysis and calculations performed are documented in HOLTEC Report HI-
2261319 Rev. 1, Structural Evaluation of Fuel Transfer Canister for Palisades Nuclear Plant.
[Reference 3] Per HI-2261319 Rev. 1, the stress criteria are satisfied, and therefore the FTC is
determined to be structurally adequate for its intended purpose.
Reference 3 evaluated the structural integrity of the FTC and demonstrated compliance with the
specified allowable stress limits. The stress analysis used static equilibrium and strength of
materials principles to evaluate potential failure modes under normal lifting and handling
conditions. The calculation used dimensions and weights listed in the FTC drawing as design
inputs, and concludes that all safety factors are greater than 1.0.
SFP Seismic Stability and Floor Loading Analysis
The FTC will be supported on a vertical support stand within the cask loading area of the SFP.
This configuration has been evaluated for seismic stability under the safe shutdown earthquake
(SSE) loading condition. The evaluation addressed the potential for overturning and sliding, and
the structural adequacy of the SFP floor slab. This evaluation is documented in HOLTEC Report
HI-2261282 Rev. 2, Seismic Stability and Floor Loading Analysis of the Fuel Transfer Canister
in the Spent Fuel Pool at Palisades [Reference 2].
The seismic stability evaluation analyzed the initial overturning and sliding stability checks using
force and moment equilibrium principles. Prior to performing the stability evaluation, the
 PNP 2026-052
Enclosure
Page 10 of 19

dynamic characteristics of the combined FTC, vertical stand, and supporting spent fuel pool
(SFP) slab are evaluated to establish the applicable spectral accelerations. The natural
frequency is determined by using Roark’s formulas for stress and strain, and the inputs to these
calculations are existing plant floor loading evaluations and weight of the fuel, FTC, and vertical
support stand. Sliding is identified as a credible failure mode, but the calculated sliding
displacement remains less than the available clearance within the Cask Loading Area (CLA)
[Reference 2].
Based on the results of the evaluation, the FTC and vertical stand remain stable against
overturning under the SSE loading condition. Furthermore, the structural evaluation
demonstrates that the calculated floor slab demands do not exceed the applicable capacities
and the SFP floor slab is demonstrated to be structurally adequate to support the configuration
under evaluated loading conditions.
Thermal Evaluation
Per HOLTEC Report HI-2261312 Rev. 0, Thermal Evaluation of Fuel Transfer Operations using
Fuel Transfer Canister at Palisades NPP [Reference 4], a steady-state 3-D Computational Fluid
Dynamics (CFD) model was used to perform thermal evaluations. The allowable fuel exposure
duration in air was determined using the cumulative oxidation usage methodology described in
the HI-STAR 80 SAR. Methodology is based on the temperature-dependent oxidation kinetics of
UO2 documented in NUREG-1565 and limits the cumulative oxidation usage to U ≤ 1.0. The
bounding fuel temperature calculated by the computational fluid dynamics analysis was used to
determine the permissible duration of fuel exposure to air.
Accordingly, the fuel transfer operation is acceptable provided that the total duration for which
the fuel is exposed to an oxidizing atmosphere during removal of the FTC from water, gravity
drainage, transfer through air, and placement in the spent fuel pool does not exceed the
prescribed duration of 133 hours. Based on the results of the thermal and fuel oxidation
evaluations, the analyzed fuel transfer operation maintains the fuel cladding temperature below
the applicable limit and restricts UO2 oxidation to acceptable levels that maintain fuel cladding
integrity during the recovery of DD41.
This evaluation demonstrates that the canister retains its integrity while carrying DD41. The
analysis was performed using FLUENT code and included the effects of conduction, natural
convection, and thermal radiation heat transfer. The methodology incorporated conservative
modeling assumptions for the fuel assembly, FTC configuration, material properties, and heat
rejection mechanisms. It has been concluded that the fuel cladding temperatures do not exceed
517˚F, which is under the 752˚F acceptance criteria.
Drop Analysis
Per HI-2261346 Rev. 0, Fuel Transfer Canister Drop Analysis [Reference 5], the structural
response of the FTC was evaluated for three bounding horizontal drop conditions using LS-
DYNA analyses which included: FTC pure horizontal impact, FTC horizontal drop with the top
end impacting first, FTC horizontal drop with the bottom end impacting first. Based on the
calculated response, the FTC maintains its overall structural configuration throughout the
evaluated impact events. All bolts have bending and shear safety factors greater than unity, and
all calculated combined-loading interaction ratios are below unity. Therefore, the bolts satisfy
the applicable strength and interaction criteria.

The results from all three simulations indicate that the FTC remains structurally adequate and
functionally intact under the evaluated bounding drop conditions. No calculated response was
identified that would compromise the FTC structure, fuel confinement boundary, closing-gate
assembly, or safe retention of the spent fuel assembly.
3.2     Assessment of Radiological Conditions
The radiological assessment considered the differences between routine underwater fuel
movement and the proposed alternate recovery and transfer of fuel assembly DD41. The
assessment addressed direct gamma and neutron radiation, occupational dose, airborne
radioactivity, contamination, installed and supplemental radiation monitoring, ventilation and
release controls, and radiological contingencies.
Detailed implementation requirements, including specific instrument locations, alarm or action
levels, personnel stay times, hold points, protective clothing, respiratory protection, and
contingency actions, are established in approved recovery procedures, Radiation Work Permits,
and the activity-specific ALARA plan.
3.2.1   Dose Comparisons
During routine fuel movement, the fuel assembly remains underwater, and the water provides
radiation shielding, cooling, neutron absorption, and retention of radioactive material. The
proposed alternate recovery involves placement of DD41 in an engineered FTC and movement
above the water surface for a controlled period.
The FTC provides engineered gamma and neutron shielding for the loaded fuel assembly. The
shielding evaluation considers the fuel source term, burnup and decay history, canister

The DD41 recovery procedure establishes a controlled and defined load path for movement of
the FTC from the reactor cavity to the SFP building, FHSO-19A, Recovery of FA DD41
[Reference 9]
Following recovery of DD41 from its tilted position, DD41 is maintained a minimum of 10 feet
underwater while being lifted from the reactor vessel and transferred laterally to the FTC. The
FMD and DD41 are moved until they are no longer directly over any portion of the reactor
vessel, after which the assembly is leveled and lowered onto the bottom section of the FTC. The

After DD41 is positioned on the FTC bottom, the top section is lowered onto the bottom section,
aligned using locating pins and corresponding lugs, and secured. The assembled and loaded
FTC has an approximate lift weight of 49,000 pounds.
Operations will use the Electronic Shift Operations Management System (eSOMS) to monitor
and document FTC out-of-water time in support of compliance with the analyzed 133 hour
exposure limit. The out-of-water clock will begin when the FTC first breaks the water surface
and end when the FTC is fully submerged in the SFP.
For transfer out of containment, the assembled FTC is raised vertically from the refueling cavity
while maintained in a horizontal orientation. Following release by Radiation Protection, the FTC
is maintained in horizontal orientation and transported along the defined transit path to the
containment equipment hatch. The canister is then placed onto the equipment hatch trolley and
transferred through the equipment hatch into the SFP building.
Once inside the SFP building, the horizontal rigging is removed, and the FTC is re-rigged for a
vertical lift. The FTC is then upended to the vertical orientation and moved to the cask laydown
area of the SFP and placed in the FTC vertical stand.
The safe load path therefore consists of the following segments:
1.  Reactor vessel to FTC: DD41 is lifted and transferred using the FMD for placement in the
FTC while maintaining at least 10 feet of water over DD41.
2.   FTC assembly: DD41 is seated in the lower section of the FTC, top section is installed and
secured, and the assembled FTC is prepared for transfer.
3.   Containment transfer: The loaded FTC is lifted from the cavity, moved horizontally along
the defined path to the equipment hatch, and placed on the equipment hatch trolley.
4.   Equipment hatch transfer: The trolley is used to move the FTC through the equipment
hatch into the SFP building.
5.     SFP building transfer: The FTC is re-rigged, upended from a horizontal to vertical
orientation, and moved to the cask laydown area of the SFP where it is secured prior to removal
of rigging.

                         Executive Summary
                         The purpose of this report is to evaluate the radiological consequences of the DD41 FHA for the
                         Palisades Nuclear Plant. The overturned fuel assembly DD41 will be recovered and lifted from
                         the reactor core and moved to a specially designed fuel transfer canister. The evaluation
                         addresses the period during which the fuel assembly loaded fuel transfer canister is removed
                         from the water, drained by gravity, and transferred through the air onto a special rail cart. The
                         purpose of this analysis is to determine the dose received by the most limiting receptors at the
                         EAB, LPZ and Control Room due to unlikely event the fuel transfer canister is dropped during
                         lifting process, to ensure regulatory compliance stated in 10 CFR 50.67 [1].
                         This assessment follows the regulatory guidance in US NRC RG 1.183 [2] and NUREG-0800
                         Section 15.0.3 [3]. The results of this assessment demonstrate that, in the unlikely event of an
                         FHA, both onsite and offsite doses would remain within acceptable limits, thereby supporting the
                         LAR submittal.

                         1.0                 INTRODUCTION
                         1.1                 Purpose
                         The purpose of this report is to evaluate the radiological consequences of the DD41 FHA for the
                         Palisades Nuclear Plant. The overturned fuel assembly DD41 will be recovered and lifted from
                         the reactor core and moved to a specially designed fuel transfer canister. The evaluation
                         addresses the period during which the fuel assembly loaded fuel transfer canister is removed
                         from the water, drained by gravity, and transferred through the air onto a special rail cart. The
                         purpose of this analysis is to determine the dose received by the most limiting receptors at the
                         EAB, LPZ and Control Room due to unlikely event the fuel transfer canister is dropped during
                         lifting process, to ensure regulatory compliance stated in 10 CFR 50.67 [1].

                         1.2                 Discussion
                         This analysis evaluates the radiological consequences associated with postulated DD41 FHA
                         event in support of the LAR submittal. The analysis provides the technical basis for characterizing
                         the potential radiological consequences of the event and supports the corresponding conclusions
                         and claims documented in LAR.
                         The analysis considers the relevant characteristics and functions of SSCs that affect the transport
                         and release of radioactive material during the FHA event. The resulting radiological consequence
                         evaluation provides supporting evidence for the treatment of the FHA event within the LAR.

                         3.2                 Accident Propagation
                         The evaluation addresses the period during which the fuel assembly loaded fuel transfer canister
                         is removed from the reactor cavity water, drained by gravity, and transferred through the air onto
                         a special rail cart. Since all of the release within the FHB would be filtered, the most limiting FHA
                         will be a release inside the containment (with the assumption that the containment equipment
                         hatch is open). In case of closed containment hatch, release within containment would also be
                         filtered via pre-filters and HEPA filters prior exiting the stack, so this analysis bounds a release in
                         containment with equipment hatch closed.
                         The event propagation for release path via containment equipment hatch is described step by
                         step below.
                                   •         The DD41 fuel assembly is placed in the transport canister and lifted.
                                   •         At the time of fuel handling, the canister is postulated to drop on the containment floor.
                                   •         The drop is postulated to damage all fuel rods of the transported fuel assembly
                                             mechanically, allowing radionuclides in the fuel-clad gap to be released.
                                   •         All the gap activity in the damaged rods is assumed to mix instantaneously and
                                             homogeneously throughout the free air volume of the containment.
                                   •         The radioactive material is released to FHB through the open containment equipment
                                             hatch.
                                   •         Radioactive material is postulated to be released into the environment via the FHB
                                             ventilation system which exhausts via the plant stack.
                                   •         The released materials from the stack become part of a plume.
                                   •         Plume traverses based on the wind speed, direction, and stability.
                                   •         The most limiting receptor at the location at the outer boundaries of EAB and LPZ absorbs
                                             radioactive material because of external exposure due to immersion in the plume and
                                             internal exposure because of inhalation of radioactive material from the plume.
                                   •         The most limiting receptors in the Control Room absorb radioactivity by internal exposure
                                             and direct shine from the atmospheric plume and filters.

                         3.4                 Source Term Modeling
                         The determination of the source term for evaluating the radiological consequences of an FHA
                         accident was performed in accordance with requirements listed in Appendix B of RG 1.183 [2].
                         This appendix provides assumptions which are acceptable to the staff of the US NRC.
                         3.4.1 Assembly Inventory
                         The inventory of fuel assembly DD41 provided by Palisades staff (see Ref. [9]) was analyzed and
                         activities of isotopes of interest were derived.
                         Since only radionuclides in the gap are available for release, only noble gases, halogens and
                         alkali metal isotopes are considered in the analysis. This is as per RG 1.183 Appendix B,
                         regulatory position 1.2 [2]. The resulting inventory can be found in Section 9.1 and Appendix A.
                         3.4.2 Extent of Fuel Damage
                         The total fission product inventory available for release is determined by multiplying the
                         radionuclide inventory in assembly with the total number (or fraction) of affected rods.
                         As per RG 1.183 [2] Appendix B, the number of fuel rods assumed to be damaged during the
                         accident should be based on a conservative analysis that considers the most limiting case. This
                         analysis should consider parameters such as the weight of a dropped fuel assembly (plus any
                         attached handling grapples), the height of the drop, and the compression, torsion, and shear
                         stresses on the irradiated fuel rods. However, given the uncertain condition of the fuel assembly
                         DD41, this type of analysis is not feasible. Thus, conservatively, it is assumed that all fuel rods
                         will be damaged and the total inventory of DD41 is used for the FHA analysis.
                         3.4.3 Release Fractions and Timings
                         The radionuclide inventory for the single assembly is subsequently modified in RADTRAD through
                         the application of radionuclide-specific release fractions and timings. Release fractions determine
                         the portion of the release of the radionuclide groups during the accident. The release timings, as
                         the name suggests, determine the timing of release for each radionuclide groups.
                         For FHA, only the radionuclides in the fuel rod void volume (plenum and pellet-to-cladding gap)
                         are available for release due to cladding breach. Table 3 of RG 1.183 [2] lists the radionuclide
                         groups residing in the fuel rod void volume that are available for release upon a cladding breach.
                         All radionuclides are assumed to be released instantaneously after initiation of the accident. This
                         is a conservative assumption.
                         3.4.4 Chemical Form
                         The chemical form of radioiodine released from the fuel to the containment atmosphere should
                         be assumed to be 95% cesium iodide (CsI), 4.85 percent elemental iodine, and 0.15 percent
                         organic iodide, as per RG 1.183 Appendix B, regulatory position 1.3 [2].

                         3.5.1 Filtered Pathways Modeling
                         Each pathway is modeled using a filter. They are described below.
                                                       3.5.1.1                       Hatch Release
                         The filter for this pathway models the open containment equipment hatch. No mitigation is
                         assumed for the pathway; hence filter efficiency is 0% for all chemical forms.
                                                       3.5.1.2                       Stack Release
                         The filters for this pathway models filtered release that exits via the FHB filtration system
                         exhausting via the plant stack. The exhaust air flows at 75000 cfm rate through the HEPA filter
                         and a charcoal filter [10]; hence filter efficiency is 94% for elemental and organic forms as per
                         Ref. [11], [12]. For the aerosol form – 99% removal efficiency is conservatively applied per
                         Palisades Filter Specification [13] (See Assumption 2 in Section 6.0).
                                                       3.5.1.1                       Control Room Unfiltered Makeup
                         The initial unfiltered makeup flow rate is 660 cfm. After control room isolation at 20 minutes, the
                         flow is 0 cfm [10]. No mitigation is assumed for the pathway; hence filter efficiency is 0% for all
                         chemical forms.
                                                       3.5.1.2                       Control Room Filtered Makeup
                         The control room filtered makeup flow of 1413.6 cfm starts at 20 minutes (time of control room
                         isolation) [10]. 99% filter efficiency is applied to all release fractions.
                                                       3.5.1.3                       Control Room Unfiltered Inleakage
                         The unfiltered inleakage was set to 100 cfm [10]. No mitigation is assumed for the pathway; hence
                         filter efficiency is 0% for all chemical forms.
                                                       3.5.1.4                       Control Room Exhaust Flow
                         The control room exhaust is equal to the sum of the control room intake and inleakage flows. No
                         mitigation is assumed for the pathway; hence filter efficiency is 0% for all chemical forms.
                                                       3.5.1.5                       Control Room Recirculation Flow
                         The control room HVAC system is assumed to be operating in normal mode at the beginning of
                         the event. The control room enters emergency mode at 20 minutes (manual operator action). So,
                         1413.6 cfm flow is applied to this filter after 20 minutes [10]. 99% filter efficiency is applied to all
                         release fractions.
                         3.5.2 Atmospheric Dispersion Modeling
                         Atmospheric dispersion (from release point to receptor points) analysis has been performed [14].
                         The Atmospheric Dispersion Coefficients (X/Qs) have been determined for the receptors:
                                   •         Individual at the most limiting EAB location
                                   •         Most limiting receptor at the outer boundary of the LPZ
                                   •         Hypothetical maximum exposed individual in Control Room
                         The factors input can be found in Appendix A.

                         4.0                 ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
                         To address the US NRC regulatory requirements stated in 10 CFR 50.67 [1], the calculation
                         methodology follows RG 1.183 [2] and NUREG-0800 Section 15.0.3 [3].
                         The dose acceptance criteria, as per the guides, are as follows:
                                             •
                                   EAB: Maximum dose in any 2-hour period in 720 hours (30 days) following the start of
                                   the radioactivity release ≤ 6.3 rem TEDE
                               • LPZ: Maximum dose in 720 hours (30 days) following the start of the radioactivity
                                   release ≤ 6.3 rem TEDE
                               • Control Room: Maximum dose in 720 hours (30 days) following the start of the
                                   radioactivity release ≤ 5 rem TEDE
                         The above requirements bound the requirements stated in 10 CFR 50.67 [1].

                         because the DBA LOCA model assumes release from the entire reactor core, whereas the FHA
                         model considers damage to only one fuel assembly with a reduced radionuclide inventory. In
                         addition, the DBA LOCA analysis includes a broader range of radionuclides than the FHA
                         analysis. Since the DBA LOCA source term is based on a larger affected fuel inventory and
                         includes all radionuclides considered in the FHA evaluation, the resulting DBA LOCA shine dose
